claim: Human African trypanosomiasis is a debilitating and fatal parasitic disease endemic to sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Human African trypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness, is a debilitating and fatal parasitic disease endemic to sub-Saharan Africa (Fevre et al., 2008; Simarro et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fevre et al., 2008 and Simarro et al., 2008

claim: Human African trypanosomiasis is caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei.
source: Caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei, the disease begins in the hemolymphatic system and later crosses the blood–brain barrier, resulting in sleep disturbances that deteriorate to coma and death.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about the causative agent of African trypanosomiasis

claim: The disease begins in the hemolymphatic system and later crosses the blood-brain barrier.
source: Caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei, the disease begins in the hemolymphatic system and later crosses the blood–brain barrier, resulting in sleep disturbances that deteriorate to coma and death.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about disease progression

claim: The disease results in sleep disturbances that deteriorate to coma and death.
source: Caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei, the disease begins in the hemolymphatic system and later crosses the blood–brain barrier, resulting in sleep disturbances that deteriorate to coma and death.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about disease symptoms and outcomes

claim: Parasites evade the host immune system through periodic switching of the variable surface glycoprotein coat.
source: During the course of infection, the parasites evade the host immune system through periodic switching of the variable surface glycoprotein coat, making vaccination-based approaches unlikely to succeed (Taylor and Rudenko, 2006; Horn and McCulloch, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor and Rudenko, 2006 and Horn and McCulloch, 2010

claim: Vaccination-based approaches are unlikely to succeed against African trypanosomiasis.
source: During the course of infection, the parasites evade the host immune system through periodic switching of the variable surface glycoprotein coat, making vaccination-based approaches unlikely to succeed (Taylor and Rudenko, 2006; Horn and McCulloch, 2010).
evidence: Inference based on the mechanism of immune evasion, supported by citations

claim: Only four chemotherapeutics are currently approved for sleeping sickness.
source: Currently, only four chemotherapeutics are approved for sleeping sickness.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about available treatments

claim: Current therapies for sleeping sickness suffer from poor oral bioavailability, severe toxicity, and/or emerging resistance.
source: These therapies suffer from poor oral bioavailability, severe toxicity, and/or emerging resistance.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about limitations of current treatments

claim: Eflornithine is the only drug with a known mechanism of action for sleeping sickness.
source: Eflornithine, the only drug with a known mechanism of action, is also the only therapeutic for sleeping sickness approved in the last 50 years (Fairlamb, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fairlamb, 2003

claim: Eflornithine is the only therapeutic for sleeping sickness approved in the last 50 years.
source: Eflornithine, the only drug with a known mechanism of action, is also the only therapeutic for sleeping sickness approved in the last 50 years (Fairlamb, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fairlamb, 2003

claim: A combination of eflornithine and nifurtimox was introduced in 2009 for T. brucei infection.
source: Although a combination of eflornithine and nifurtimox, a drug for American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease, caused by T. cruzi), was introduced in 2009 for T. brucei infection, no new drugs are near the clinic (Priotto et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Priotto et al., 2009

claim: No new drugs for African trypanosomiasis are near the clinic.
source: Although a combination of eflornithine and nifurtimox, a drug for American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease, caused by T. cruzi), was introduced in 2009 for T. brucei infection, no new drugs are near the clinic (Priotto et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Priotto et al., 2009

claim: More than 15 kinase inhibitors have received FDA approval during the past decade.
source: Protein kinases have been intensely pursued as therapeutic targets for cancer and autoimmune disease, and more than 15 kinase inhibitors have received FDA approval during the past decade.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about FDA-approved kinase inhibitors

claim: Protein phosphorylation in T. brucei is an essential regulatory mechanism.
source: As in humans, protein phosphorylation in T. brucei is an essential regulatory mechanism and plays critical but poorly understood roles in its unique life cycle (Parsons et al., 2005; Nett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parsons et al., 2005 and Nett et al., 2009

claim: Protein phosphorylation plays critical but poorly understood roles in the T. brucei life cycle.
source: As in humans, protein phosphorylation in T. brucei is an essential regulatory mechanism and plays critical but poorly understood roles in its unique life cycle (Parsons et al., 2005; Nett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parsons et al., 2005 and Nett et al., 2009

claim: T. brucei has 182 protein kinases.
source: The vast majority of the 182 protein kinases in T. brucei remain poorly characterized, and few have been interrogated in their native cellular context with small-molecule inhibitors.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about the T. brucei kinome

claim: The vast majority of T. brucei protein kinases remain poorly characterized.
source: The vast majority of the 182 protein kinases in T. brucei remain poorly characterized, and few have been interrogated in their native cellular context with small-molecule inhibitors.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Few T. brucei kinases have been interrogated in their native cellular context with small-molecule inhibitors.
source: The vast majority of the 182 protein kinases in T. brucei remain poorly characterized, and few have been interrogated in their native cellular context with small-molecule inhibitors.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: SCYX-5070 is the first reported protein kinase inhibitor with efficacy in a murine model of T. brucei infection.
source: High-throughput screening and medicinal chemistry recently led to the discovery of SCYX-5070, the first reported protein kinase inhibitor with efficacy in a murine model of T. brucei infection (Mercer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mercer et al., 2011

claim: SCYX-5070 binds at least six trypanosome kinases related to human MAPKs and cyclin-dependent kinases.
source: Affinity chromatography with an immobilized derivative suggested that SCYX-5070 binds at least six trypanosome kinases related to human mitogen activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and cyclin-dependent kinases, although the extent to which SCYX-5070 engages these kinases in vivo is not known.
evidence: Based on affinity chromatography experiments, but with uncertainty about in vivo engagement

claim: The extent to which SCYX-5070 engages its target kinases in vivo is not known.
source: Affinity chromatography with an immobilized derivative suggested that SCYX-5070 binds at least six trypanosome kinases related to human mitogen activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and cyclin-dependent kinases, although the extent to which SCYX-5070 engages these kinases in vivo is not known.
evidence: Acknowledgment of a gap in knowledge

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinases are essential in T. brucei.
source: Genetic studies in T. brucei have established essential roles for orthologs of several human kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinases (Tu and Wang, 2004; Gourguechon and Wang, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tu and Wang, 2004 and Gourguechon and Wang, 2009

claim: Aurora kinase is essential in T. brucei.
source: Genetic studies in T. brucei have established essential roles for orthologs of several human kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinases (Tu and Wang, 2004; Gourguechon and Wang, 2009), Aurora kinase (Tu et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2006

claim: Polo-like kinase is essential in T. brucei.
source: polo-like kinase (Li et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2010

claim: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 is essential in T. brucei.
source: glycogen synthase kinase-3 (Ojo et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ojo et al., 2008

claim: Casein kinase-1 is essential in T. brucei.
source: casein kinase-1 (Urbaniak, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Urbaniak, 2009

claim: DBF-2-related kinases are essential in T. brucei.
source: DBF-2-related kinases (Ma et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2010

claim: High-throughput RNAi studies have implicated additional kinases in T. brucei proliferation.
source: High-throughput RNAi studies have implicated additional kinases in T. brucei proliferation (Alsford et al., 2011; Mackey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alsford et al., 2011 and Mackey et al., 2011

claim: It is not clear which T. brucei kinases make the best therapeutic targets.
source: Despite the knowledge gained from these studies, it is not clear which T. brucei kinases make the best therapeutic targets.
evidence: Assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Achieving sufficient potency to inhibit essential T. brucei kinases while avoiding related human kinases poses a significant challenge.
source: Achieving sufficient potency to inhibit essential T. brucei kinases, while avoiding related human kinases, poses a significant challenge.
evidence: Assessment of challenges in drug development

claim: Quantifying intracellular kinase engagement by small-molecule inhibitors in T. brucei is an unsolved problem.
source: Moreover, quantifying intracellular kinase engagement by small-molecule inhibitors in T. brucei is an unsolved problem.
evidence: Assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Hypothemycin is a polyketide natural product.
source: Hypothemycin (1, Figure 1A) is a polyketide natural product that covalently inhibits a diverse subset of human kinases, including MEK, ERK, PDGFR, VEGFR2, and FLT3 (Schirmer et al., 2006; Winssinger and Barluenga, 2007).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about hypothemycin

claim: Hypothemycin covalently inhibits a diverse subset of human kinases including MEK, ERK, PDGFR, VEGFR2, and FLT3.
source: Hypothemycin (1, Figure 1A) is a polyketide natural product that covalently inhibits a diverse subset of human kinases, including MEK, ERK, PDGFR, VEGFR2, and FLT3 (Schirmer et al., 2006; Winssinger and Barluenga, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schirmer et al., 2006 and Winssinger and Barluenga, 2007

claim: Hypothemycin has antitumor activity in mouse xenograft models.
source: Hypothemycin (Tanaka et al., 1999) and related compounds (Barluenga et al., 2010) have antitumor activity in mouse xenograft models, and one variant has entered clinical trials (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 1999 and Barluenga et al., 2010

claim: One hypothemycin variant has entered clinical trials.
source: Hypothemycin (Tanaka et al., 1999) and related compounds (Barluenga et al., 2010) have antitumor activity in mouse xenograft models, and one variant has entered clinical trials (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2011

claim: All hypothemycin-sensitive kinases have a common cysteine immediately preceding the catalytic DXG motif.
source: All hypothemycin-sensitive kinases have a common cysteine immediately preceding the catalytic DXG motif (where X is usually Phe or Leu) (Schirmer et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schirmer et al., 2006

claim: A homologous CDXG motif is present in 48 of 518 human protein kinases.
source: A homologous CDXG motif is present in 48 of 518 human protein kinases (Leproult et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leproult et al., 2011

claim: CDXG kinases are functionally diverse, encompassing Tyr, Ser/Thr, and dual-specificity kinases distributed throughout the kinome phylogenetic tree.
source: CDXG kinases are functionally diverse, encompassing Tyr, Ser/Thr, and dual-specificity kinases distributed throughout the kinome phylogenetic tree.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about CDXG kinases

claim: The nucleophilic thiol of hypothemycin-sensitive CDXG kinases undergoes conjugate addition to the cis-enone.
source: The nucleophilic thiol of hypothemycin-sensitive CDXG kinases undergoes conjugate addition to the cis-enone, as revealed by a crystal structure of the ERK2/hypothemycin complex (Rastelli et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rastelli et al., 2008 describing crystal structure

claim: The CDXG motif is necessary for potent inhibition by hypothemycin.
source: While the CDXG motif is necessary for potent inhibition by hypothemycin, it does not appear to be sufficient.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: The CDXG motif is not sufficient for potent inhibition by hypothemycin.
source: While the CDXG motif is necessary for potent inhibition by hypothemycin, it does not appear to be sufficient.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: One-third of human CDXG kinases were unaffected by hypothemycin variants screened at 1 μM.
source: One-third of human CDXG kinases were unaffected by hypothemycin variants screened at a concentration of 1 μM (Barluenga et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barluenga et al., 2010

claim: The selectivity of hypothemycin toward endogenous kinases in living cells remains unknown.
source: The selectivity of hypothemycin toward endogenous kinases in living cells remains unknown.
evidence: Assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Approximately ten percent of T. brucei kinases (21 of 182) have a CDXG motif.
source: Similar to humans, approximately ten percent of T. brucei kinases (21 of 182) have a CDXG motif.
evidence: Based on analysis of the T. brucei kinome

claim: Hypothemycin kills bloodstream form T. brucei with an EC50 of approximately 170 nM.
source: Treatment of bloodstream form (BSF) parasites with increasing concentrations of hypothemycin for 24 hr caused a sharp reduction in cell density (EC50 ∼ 170 nM, Figure 1B), principally resulting from cell death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Hypothemycin treatment of T. brucei principally results in cell death.
source: Treatment of bloodstream form (BSF) parasites with increasing concentrations of hypothemycin for 24 hr caused a sharp reduction in cell density (EC50 ∼ 170 nM, Figure 1B), principally resulting from cell death.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Cells treated for 5 hr with 500 nM hypothemycin were round and swollen, with the flagellum detached from the cell body.
source: Visual inspection revealed that cells treated for 5 hr with 500 nM hypothemycin were round and swollen, with the flagellum detached from the cell body.
evidence: Based on visual inspection of treated cells

claim: T. brucei cells treated with hypothemycin died within 2 hr and did not recover when transferred to drug-free media.
source: They died within 2 hr and did not recover even when transferred to media lacking hypothemycin (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Infected mice showed a dose-dependent reduction in parasitemia when treated with hypothemycin.
source: Infected mice showed a dose-dependent reduction in parasitemia (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A 10 mg/kg dose of hypothemycin administered once daily for 7 days prolonged survival of infected mice over 30 days with a cure rate of 33%.
source: a 10 mg/kg dose administered once daily for 7 days prolonged survival of infected mice over 30 days, with a cure rate of 33% (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: At doses of 10 mg/kg or higher, signs of toxicity were evident in infected animals.
source: At a dose of 10 mg/kg or higher, signs of toxicity were evident in infected animals (weight loss, lethargy), precluding more aggressive dosing regimens.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in mice

claim: Hypothemycin's therapeutic window is narrow, likely due to inhibition of essential mammalian CDXG kinases.
source: Although hypothemycin's therapeutic window is narrow, likely due to inhibition of essential mammalian CDXG kinases (e.g., VEGFR2, MEK1/2), its potent trypanocidal activity in vitro and in vivo motivated us to search for trypanosomal hypothemycin-binding proteins.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and known targets

claim: In the crystal structure of hypothemycin bound to ERK2, the C4 methyl ether is solvent exposed.
source: In the crystal structure of hypothemycin bound to ERK2, the C4 methyl ether is solvent exposed (Rastelli et al., 2008), suggesting that this and other kinases would accommodate a larger group at this position (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rastelli et al., 2008 and shown in Figure 2A

claim: Probe 2 (propargyl-hypothemycin) is equipotent to hypothemycin against cultured BSF T. brucei.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, probe 2 was equipotent to hypothemycin against cultured BSF T. brucei (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Labeling of a 43 kDa protein by probe 2 was detected with 25 nM and reached maximum intensity at 500 nM.
source: Labeling of a 43 kDa protein was detected with 25 nM 2, reaching maximum intensity at 500 nM (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: Labeled bands at 50 and 90 kDa failed to saturate and are likely nonspecific adducts.
source: Labeled bands at 50 and 90 kDa were apparent at higher concentrations, but they failed to saturate (Figure 2E) and are likely nonspecific adducts.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E and inference about specificity

claim: Pretreating lysates with increasing concentrations of hypothemycin abolished subsequent labeling of the 43 kDa band.
source: Pretreating lysates with increasing concentrations of hypothemycin abolished subsequent labeling of the 43 kDa band, demonstrating that it is a specific and saturable hypothemycin target (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The 43 kDa band is a specific and saturable hypothemycin target.
source: Pretreating lysates with increasing concentrations of hypothemycin abolished subsequent labeling of the 43 kDa band, demonstrating that it is a specific and saturable hypothemycin target (Figure 2F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating competition

claim: TbGSK3short is the dominant protein in the 43 kDa band labeled by probe 2.
source: After SDS-PAGE, analysis of the 43 kDa band by mass spectrometry identified the dominant protein (based on total peptide counts) as TbGSK3short (Tb927.10.13780), a CDXG kinase previously found to be essential in BSF T. brucei (Ojo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to Ojo et al., 2008

claim: TbGSK3short was previously found to be essential in BSF T. brucei.
source: After SDS-PAGE, analysis of the 43 kDa band by mass spectrometry identified the dominant protein (based on total peptide counts) as TbGSK3short (Tb927.10.13780), a CDXG kinase previously found to be essential in BSF T. brucei (Ojo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ojo et al., 2008

claim: Peptides from three other CDXG kinases were detected in the 43 kDa gel band.
source: Peptides from three other CDXG kinases were also detected in the same gel band (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1A

claim: Of 21 predicted CDXG kinases, 11 were identified by probe 2 after affinity purification from cell lysates.
source: Of 21 predicted CDXG kinases, 11 were identified by probe 2 after affinity purification from cell lysates.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from the chemoproteomic experiment

claim: Every protein kinase identified by probe 2 contains the CDXG motif.
source: Of note, every protein kinase identified by probe 2 contains the CDXG motif, accounting for over half of the 21 CDXG kinases encoded in the T. brucei genome.
evidence: Based on analysis of identified kinases

claim: This represents the first unbiased identification of hypothemycin-binding proteins.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first unbiased identification of hypothemycin-binding proteins.
evidence: Assessment of novelty relative to prior work

claim: Fragmentation spectra of peptides derived from eight kinases provided iTRAQ reporter ions of sufficient intensity to quantify kinase recovery.
source: Fragmentation spectra of peptides derived from eight kinases provided iTRAQ reporter ions of sufficient intensity to quantify kinase recovery (i.e., labeling by 2) as a function of hypothemycin pretreatment (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: Hypothemycin pretreatment did not affect recovery of non-kinase proteins like tubulin, heat shock proteins, and ribosomal proteins.
source: In addition to CDXG kinases, several other proteins (e.g., tubulin, heat shock proteins, ribosomal proteins) were identified. However, hypothemycin pretreatment did not affect their recovery (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1A), which likely resulted from nonspecific, low-level modification by 2 and/or nonspecific adsorption to the avidin-agarose beads.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1A

claim: Recovery of TbCLK1/2 was uniquely affected by pretreatment with 20 nM hypothemycin.
source: Among the CDXG kinases quantified, recovery of TbCLK1/2 was uniquely affected by pretreatment with 20 nM hypothemycin (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by iTRAQ quantification data shown in Figure 3

claim: Recovery of TbGSK3short and TbMAPK2 was reduced more than 50% by 200 nM hypothemycin.
source: Recovery of two additional kinases, TbGSK3short (Tb927.10.13780) and TbMAPK2 (Tb927.10.16030), was reduced more than 50% by 200 nM hypothemycin
evidence: Supported by iTRAQ quantification data

claim: Recovery of all but one CDXG kinase was reduced by 1 μM hypothemycin.
source: and recovery of all but one CDXG kinase was reduced by 1 μM.
evidence: Supported by iTRAQ quantification data

claim: TbCLK1/2 exhibits greater sensitivity to hypothemycin than TbGSK3short and TbMAPK2.
source: These data indicate a wide range of hypothemycin sensitivity, with TbCLK1/2 exhibiting somewhat greater sensitivity than TbGSK3short and TbMAPK2.
evidence: Based on comparison of iTRAQ quantification data

claim: TbMAPK2 is not essential in BSF T. brucei.
source: TbMAPK2 is not essential in BSF T. brucei but is required for proliferation of the procyclic (insect host) form (Muller et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller et al., 2002

claim: TbMAPK2 is required for proliferation of the procyclic form of T. brucei.
source: TbMAPK2 is not essential in BSF T. brucei but is required for proliferation of the procyclic (insect host) form (Muller et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller et al., 2002

claim: TbCLK1 and TbCLK2 have identical kinase domains and only diverge in their N-terminal regions.
source: TbCLK1 and TbCLK2, which have identical kinase domains and only diverge in their N-terminal regions, are presumed to be equally sensitive to hypothemycin.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: TbCLK1 and TbCLK2 are presumed to be equally sensitive to hypothemycin.
source: TbCLK1 and TbCLK2, which have identical kinase domains and only diverge in their N-terminal regions, are presumed to be equally sensitive to hypothemycin.
evidence: Based on inference from their identical kinase domains

claim: Knockdown of TbGSK3short reduced cell viability.
source: Consistent with previous results (Ojo et al., 2008), we observed reduced viability after knockdown of TbGSK3short (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Ojo et al., 2008

claim: Knockdown of TbMAPK2, Tb927.6.1780, and Tb927.6.4220 had no effect on cell viability.
source: Also consistent with previous studies, knockdown of MAP kinases TbMAPK2 (Muller et al., 2002), Tb927.6.1780 (Guttinger et al., 2007), and Tb927.6.4220 (Domenicali Pfister et al., 2006) had no effect on cell viability (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1B, and citations to previous studies

claim: Knockdown of TbCLK1 resulted in reduced proliferation and increased cell death.
source: Induction with tetracycline resulted in reduced proliferation and increased cell death (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: A lethal phenotype was only observed after knockdown of TbCLK1, not TbCLK2.
source: To test for nonredundant functions of TbCLK1 and TbCLK2, we designed a set of RNAi constructs targeting the unique 5′-UTR of each gene. A lethal phenotype was only observed after knockdown of TbCLK1; knockdown of TbCLK2 had no obvious effect (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by RNAi data shown in Figures 4C and 4D

claim: Knockdown of TbCLK2 had no obvious effect on cell proliferation.
source: A lethal phenotype was only observed after knockdown of TbCLK1; knockdown of TbCLK2 had no obvious effect (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by RNAi data shown in Figures 4C and 4D

claim: Individual knockdown of the remaining CDXG kinases had no effect on cell proliferation.
source: Individual knockdown of the remaining CDXG kinases similarly had no effect on cell proliferation.
evidence: Based on RNAi experiments

claim: Knockdown of CDXG kinase mRNAs was confirmed by quantitative PCR with 55-80% reduction across 21 mRNAs.
source: In each case, knockdown of the corresponding mRNA was confirmed by quantitative PCR (55–80% reduction across 21 mRNAs, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Supplementary file 1B

claim: TbGSK3short and TbCLK1 are the only essential CDXG kinases in BSF T. brucei.
source: With the caveat that insufficient knockdown may underlie the lack of a proliferation defect in certain cases, these results suggest that TbGSK3short and TbCLK1 are the only essential CDXG kinases in BSF T. brucei.
evidence: Based on inference from RNAi data with acknowledgment of limitations

claim: Hypothemycin inhibited TbCLK1 with an IC50 of 150 nM when pre-incubated for 30 min in the presence of 100 μM ATP.
source: Hypothemycin inhibited TbCLK1 with an IC50 of 150 nM when pre-incubated for 30 min in the presence of 100 μM ATP, whereas inhibition of TbGSK3short required 30-fold higher concentrations under the same conditions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Inhibition of TbGSK3short by hypothemycin required 30-fold higher concentrations than TbCLK1 under the same conditions.
source: Hypothemycin inhibited TbCLK1 with an IC50 of 150 nM when pre-incubated for 30 min in the presence of 100 μM ATP, whereas inhibition of TbGSK3short required 30-fold higher concentrations under the same conditions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Treatment of intact cells with 500 nM hypothemycin for 5 hr resulted in death of the vast majority of cells.
source: Moreover, the concentration dependence of this effect (reduction of labeling) correlated with the loss of cell viability; the vast majority of cells treated for 5 hr with 500 nM hypothemycin died.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Hypothemycin had a negligible effect on HA-tagged TbGSK3short in intact cells, even at the highest concentration tested.
source: In contrast to its potent effect on TbCLK1, hypothemycin had a negligible effect on HA-tagged TbGSK3short, even at the highest concentration tested.
evidence: Supported by cellular labeling data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Inhibition of TbCLK1, rather than TbGSK3short, plays a more dominant role in mediating the cytotoxic effects of hypothemycin.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that inhibition of TbCLK1, rather than TbGSK3short, plays a more dominant role in mediating the cytotoxic effects of hypothemycin.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: Hypothemycin-mediated toxicity may be caused by inactivation of MEK and VEGFR2.
source: Hypothemycin-mediated toxicity may be caused by inactivation of MEK and VEGFR2, as previous studies have found toxic effects associated with selective inhibitors of these kinases (Rugo et al., 2005; Adjei et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from previous studies, supported by citations to Rugo et al., 2005 and Adjei et al., 2008

claim: Trypanosomes lack orthologs of most hypothemycin-sensitive mammalian kinases, including MEK and VEGFR2.
source: Trypanosomes lack orthologs of most hypothemycin-sensitive mammalian kinases, including MEK and VEGFR2.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: The majority of CDXG kinases in T. brucei lack clear human orthologs.
source: Conversely, the majority of CDXG kinases in T. brucei lack clear human orthologs.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: It is likely that the remaining CDXG kinases not identified by probe 2 are not efficiently labeled or are not expressed in BSF T. brucei.
source: It is likely that the remaining CDXG kinases are not efficiently labeled by 2 or are not expressed in BSF T. brucei.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: TbGSK3short was previously shown to be essential for proliferation and survival of BSF T. brucei.
source: TbGSK3short was previously shown to be essential for proliferation and survival of BSF T. brucei (Ojo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ojo et al., 2008

claim: High-throughput screening with recombinant TbGSK3short has provided inhibitors with high biochemical potency yet modest selectivity against human GSK3β.
source: High-throughput screening with recombinant TbGSK3short has provided inhibitors with high biochemical potency, yet modest selectivity when tested against human GSK3β (Oduor et al., 2011; Urbaniak et al., 2012), consistent with the high sequence similarity shared by these kinases.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oduor et al., 2011 and Urbaniak et al., 2012

claim: It is unclear whether TbGSK3short inhibitors actually inhibit TbGSK3short in cells.
source: Although many of these compounds block T. brucei proliferation, it is unclear whether they actually inhibit TbGSK3short in cells.
evidence: Assessment of uncertainty in the field

claim: Hypothemycin was able to saturate TbGSK3short at nanomolar concentrations in cell lysates.
source: Indeed, hypothemycin was able to saturate TbGSK3short at nanomolar concentrations in cell lysates, yet it had little effect on this kinase in intact cells, even after prolonged treatment at cytotoxic concentrations.
evidence: Based on experimental data from lysate labeling experiments

claim: Hypothemycin had little effect on TbGSK3short in intact cells, even after prolonged treatment at cytotoxic concentrations.
source: Indeed, hypothemycin was able to saturate TbGSK3short at nanomolar concentrations in cell lysates, yet it had little effect on this kinase in intact cells, even after prolonged treatment at cytotoxic concentrations.
evidence: Based on experimental data from cellular labeling experiments

claim: It is unlikely that hypothemycin kills T. brucei by inhibiting TbGSK3short.
source: Thus, despite TbGSK3short being the most prominent protein labeled by 2 in lysates, it is unlikely that hypothemycin kills T. brucei by inhibiting TbGSK3short.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing lack of engagement in intact cells

claim: TbCLK1 silencing by RNAi is sufficient to kill T. brucei.
source: Together with the demonstration that TbCLK1 silencing by RNAi is sufficient to kill T. brucei, these results validate TbCLK1 as a druggable target.
evidence: Based on RNAi experimental data

claim: TbCLK1 is validated as a druggable target.
source: Together with the demonstration that TbCLK1 silencing by RNAi is sufficient to kill T. brucei, these results validate TbCLK1 as a druggable target.
evidence: Based on inference from RNAi data and target engagement data

claim: T. brucei and other kinetoplastids are the only organisms in which a CLK ortholog bears a CDXG motif.
source: T. brucei and other kinetoplastids, including the human pathogens T. cruzi and Leishmania species, are the only organisms in which a CLK ortholog bears a CDXG motif.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: The kinase domains of TbCLK1 and human CLK1-4 share only 30% sequence identity.
source: The kinase domains of TbCLK1 and human CLK1-4 share only 30% sequence identity.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: T. brucei and human GSK3 share 52% sequence identity, including the CDXG motif.
source: By contrast, T. brucei and human GSK3 share 52% sequence identity, including the CDXG motif.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: Obtaining inhibitors that discriminate between T. brucei and human CLK may be more straightforward compared to GSK3.
source: Obtaining inhibitors that discriminate between T. brucei and human CLK may therefore be more straightforward as compared to GSK3.
evidence: Based on inference from sequence identity differences

claim: CLKs regulate pre-mRNA splicing in fission yeast, flies, and human cells.
source: CLKs have been shown to regulate pre-mRNA splicing in fission yeast (Tang et al., 2011), flies (Du et al., 1998), and human cells (Muraki et al., 2004; Karlas et al., 2010; Fedorov et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Recent studies have revealed important splicing-independent roles for CLKs.
source: and recent studies have revealed important splicing-independent roles (Rodgers et al., 2010, 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodgers et al., 2010, 2011 and Lee et al., 2012

claim: TbCLK1 was not among the 57 kinases identified in T. brucei cell lysates using Kinobeads.
source: We note that TbCLK1 was not among the 57 kinases identified in T. brucei cell lysates using broad-spectrum kinase inhibitors immobilized on 'Kinobeads' (Urbaniak et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Urbaniak et al., 2012

claim: Kinobeads have the advantage of profiling a larger swath of the kinome.
source: Although Kinobeads and other powerful chemoproteomic platforms (Patricelli et al., 2011) have the advantage of profiling a larger swath of the kinome
evidence: Assessment of the capabilities of different chemoproteomic platforms

claim: A potential disadvantage of Kinobeads is that the probes only work in cell lysates and cannot be used to quantify kinase occupancy in intact parasites.
source: a potential disadvantage is that the probes only work in cell lysates and cannot be used to quantify kinase occupancy in intact parasites.
evidence: Assessment of limitations of different chemoproteomic platforms

claim: Probe 2 can be used to explore the related CDXG kinomes of T. cruzi and Leishmania.
source: More broadly, probe 2 and the chemoproteomic methodology described herein can be used to explore the related CDXG kinomes of T. cruzi and Leishmania, as well as uncharted kinomes in other disease-causing eukaryotes, all of which express diverse CDXG kinases.
evidence: Speculation about potential future applications

claim: Many human CDXG kinases are validated or potential drug targets.
source: Finally, many human CDXG kinases are validated or potential drug targets (e.g., MEK, ERK, VEGFR2, c-KIT, FLT3, PDGFR, TAK1, MNK)
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about human kinase drug targets

claim: Probe 2 may prove valuable in quantifying intracellular engagement of human CDXG kinases by candidate inhibitors.
source: and probe 2 may prove valuable in quantifying their intracellular engagement by candidate inhibitors.
evidence: Speculation about potential future applications

claim: TbCLK1 migrated as two major species which collapsed to a single band upon treatment with hypothemycin.
source: In control cells, TbCLK1 migrated as two major species (likely corresponding to differentially phosphorylated forms, our unpublished results), which collapsed to a single band upon treatment with hypothemycin (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The two major TbCLK1 species likely correspond to differentially phosphorylated forms.
source: In control cells, TbCLK1 migrated as two major species (likely corresponding to differentially phosphorylated forms, our unpublished results)
evidence: Based on inference from unpublished results

claim: Probe 2 labeled both TbCLK1 bands in DMSO-treated cells.
source: Probe 2 labeled both TbCLK1 bands in the DMSO-treated cells, but labeling was sharply reduced in cells pretreated with hypothemycin.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Labeling of TbCLK1 by probe 2 was sharply reduced in cells pretreated with hypothemycin.
source: Probe 2 labeled both TbCLK1 bands in the DMSO-treated cells, but labeling was sharply reduced in cells pretreated with hypothemycin.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The concentration dependence of reduced TbCLK1 labeling correlated with the loss of cell viability.
source: Moreover, the concentration dependence of this effect (reduction of labeling) correlated with the loss of cell viability
evidence: Based on comparison of labeling data and cell viability data
